'''''Miscanthus''''', or '''silvergrass'',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=MISCA|taxon=Miscanthus|access-date=13 July 2015}}</ref>'' '''is a [[genus]] of African, Eurasian, and [[Pacific Island]] plants in the grass family, [[Poaceae]].<ref>Andersson, Nils Johan. 1855.  Öfversigt af Förhandlingar: Kongl. Svenska Vetenskaps-Akademien 12: 165.</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=120798 Flora of China Vol. 22 Page 581  <big>芒属</big> mang shu ''Miscanthus'' Andersson, Öfvers. Kongl. Vetensk.-Akad. Förh. 12: 165. 1855. ]</ref> The name is derived from the Greek words "''miskos"'', meaning "stem", and '''"'''''anthos"'', meaning "flower", in reference to the stalked spikelets on plants of this genus.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Miscanthus floridulus - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=285399&isprofile=0&letter=M#:~:text=Noteworthy%20Characteristics,reference%20to%20the%20stalked%20spikelets. |access-date=2024-09-25 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> Several species are known for their height and biomass production, and may be used as ornamental grasses.

* ''Miscanthus cotulifer – [[Spodiopogon cotulifer]]''
* ''Miscanthus junceus'' – ''[[Miscanthidium junceum]]''
* ''Miscanthus polydactylos – [[Stapfochloa elata]]'' 
* ''Miscanthus rufipilus – [[Saccharum rufipilum]]'' 
* ''Miscanthus tanakae – [[Pseudopogonatherum speciosum]]''
* ''Miscanthus violaceus'' <small>(K.Schum.) Pilg.</small> – ''[[Miscanthidium violaceum]]'' {{small|(K.Schum.) Robyns}}

== Physiology ==
A wide variety in [[cold tolerance]] occurs in the genus. ''M.'' × ''giganteus'' is especially vulnerable to cold, and a [[cultivar]] of ''M. sinensis'' has the best known cold tolerance.<ref name="Carroll-Somerville-2009">{{cite journal | last1=Carroll | first1=Andrew | last2=Somerville | first2=Chris | title=Cellulosic Biofuels | journal=[[Annual Review of Plant Biology]] | publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] | volume=60 | issue=1 | date=2009-06-01 | issn=1543-5008 | doi=10.1146/annurev.arplant.043008.092125 | pages=165–182| pmid=19014348 }}</ref>

== ''Miscanthus sinensis'' ==
[[File:WinterMiscanthus.jpg|thumb|Winter miscanthus, an ornamental grass, growing in southern Ontario, Canada]]

{{Main|Miscanthus sinensis}}
''M. sinensis'' is widely cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], and is the source of several cultivars. In Japan, where it is known as ''susuki'' (すすき), it is considered an iconic plant of late summer and early autumn. It is mentioned in the ''[[Man'yōshū]]'' (VIII:1538) as one of the [[Nanakusa-no-sekku#Seven Autumn Flowers|seven autumn flowers]] (''aki no nana kusa'', 秋の七草). It is used for the eighth month in ''[[hanafuda]]'' playing cards. It is decorated with [[bush clover]] for the [[Mid-Autumn Festival]]. Miscanthus has also excellent [[fiber]] properties for [[papermaking]].

== ''Miscanthus'' × ''giganteus'' ==
[[File:Miscanthus Bestand.JPG|thumb|''M.'' × ''giganteus'', an energy crop, growing in Germany]]
{{Main|Miscanthus × giganteus|label 1=Miscanthus ''×'' giganteus}}
[[Miscanthus × giganteus|''Miscanthus'' × ''giganteus'']] (''Miscanthus giganteus'', giant miscanthus)<ref group="A" name="Mg-tax">p.{{spaces}}71, "Recent classification work at the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, England has designated it as ''M.'' x ''giganteus'' […], a hybrid of ''M. sinensis'' […] and ''M. sacchariflorus'' […]"</ref> is a highly productive, rhizomatous C4 perennial grass, originating from Asia.<ref group="A" name="Mg-prod">p.{{spaces}}71, "''M.'' × ''giganteus'' is a highly productive, sterile, rhizomatous C4 perennial grass that was collected in Yokahama, Japan, in 1935 by Aksel Olsen. It was taken to Denmark, where it was cultivated and spread throughout Europe and into North America for planting in horticultural settings."</ref> 
It is a sterile (noninvasive) [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] of ''M. sinensis'' and ''M. sacchariflorus,'' and grows to heights of more than {{convert|4|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} in one growing season (from the third season onwards). In temperate climates such as in Europe, the dry mass [[Crop yield|yield]] is {{convert|10|-|40|MT/ha|ST/acre}} per year, depending on location.<ref group="A" name="Mg-yield">p.{{spaces}}79, "The majority of the literature reporting dry biomass yield for ''M.'' × ''giganteus'' originates from European studies. Ceiling peak biomass yields in established stands of ''M.'' x ''giganteus'' have approached 40 t dry matter (DM) ha<sup>−1</sup> in some European locations, although it may take 3–5 years to achieve these ceiling yields [84]. Across Europe, harvestable yields of up to 25 t DM ha-1 from established stands of ''M.'' × ''giganteus'' have been reported in areas between central Germany and southern Italy, while peak yields in central and northern Europe have ranged between 10–25 t DM ha-1, and in excess of 30 t DM ha-1 in southern Europe [3]. A quantitative review of established ''M.'' × ''giganteus'' stands across Europe reported a mean peak biomass yield of 22 t DM ha-1, averaged across N rates and precipitation levels [1]."</ref> Just like ''[[Pennisetum purpureum]]'' and ''[[Saccharum ravennae]]'' (which grow to the same height), it is also called "elephant grass".

Miscanthus is mainly used for heat and power,<ref>[https://terravesta.com/who-is-terravesta/#heat_and_power "Terravesta, the first Miscanthus biomass supplier in the UK"]</ref> but can also be used as input for ethanol production (if harvested wet). If harvested dry, it can be burnt directly in biomass boilers, or processed further (pellets, briquettes). It can also be used as a "green" building material, for both wall construction and as general insulation. An experimental house based on ''Miscanthus'' straw bales was built in 2017.<ref>Blog of [[Centre for Alternative Technology|Centre for Alternative Technology in Wales:]] [http://blog.cat.org.uk/2017/09/01/worlds-first-miscanthus-bale-house/ "The world's first Miscanthus bale house"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201041907/http://blog.cat.org.uk/2017/09/01/worlds-first-miscanthus-bale-house/ |date=2017-12-01 }}.
